facts.statement: The genus Pachyornis was first described by Richard Lydekker in 1891.
Fossils of Pachyornis date from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene.
Pachyornis geranoides is the type species of the genus Pachyornis.
Pachyornis is an extinct genus of flightless ratites from New Zealand belonging to the moa family.
facts.quote: Pachyornis (from Ancient Greek παχύς (pakhús), meaning "thick", and ὄρνις (órnis), meaning "bird") is an extinct genus of ratites from New Zealand which belongs to the moa family.

facts.statement: Pachyornis was a flightless bird with a sternum lacking a keel, a trait shared by all ratites.
facts.quote: Like all ratites, Pachyornis is a flightless bird with a sternum that lacks a keel.

facts.statement: Pachyornis possessed a distinctive palate structure.
facts.quote: They also have a distinctive palate.

facts.statement: Three species of Pachyornis are currently recognized: P. geranoides, P. elephantopus, and P. australis.
facts.quote: The genus currently contains three recognised species: the type species, Pachyornis geranoides, P. elephantopus and P. australis.

facts.statement: Two distinct genetic lineages found in the North and South Islands suggest the genus might eventually be expanded to five species.
facts.quote: Two distinct genetic lineages, one each recovered from the North and South Island, could possibly expand this number to five in the future.

facts.statement: P. elephantopus is considered the species with the most extreme morphology within the genus Pachyornis.
facts.quote: the species that exhibits the most extreme morphology of the genus is the heavy-footed moa P. elephantopus.

facts.statement: Pachyornis resembled eastern moa or broad-billed moa but was distinguished by a pointed bill and a heavier build.
facts.quote: Pachyornis was generally similar to the eastern moa of the genus Emeus or the broad-billed moa of the genus Euryapteryx, but differed in having a pointed bill and being more heavyset.

facts.statement: Pachyornis species went extinct after human colonization of New Zealand, though P. australis may have died out earlier.
facts.quote: The species went extinct following human colonization of New Zealand, with the possible exception of P. australis, which may have already been extinct by then.

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Pachyornis is the family Emeidae.
Pachyornis lived from the Gelasian epoch to the Holocene, spanning 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Gelasian to Holocene (2.58 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 24 recorded fossil occurrences of Pachyornis in the Paleobiology Database.
